Paper · 23 Jul 2026

Indus-style farming went on in the Ghaggar basin after the 4.2 ka drought

Swaroop, Srivastava and colleagues · Vegetation History and Archaeobotany

In a sentence

Directly dated crops at Jognakhera, a Bara-culture site, show the Indus crop package continuing after the drought.

In plain words

About 4,200 years ago a long drought hit the region. At Jognakhera, farmers afterwards still grew the same summer and winter crops as Indus farmers. A directly dated rice grain hints at contact with the Ganga plain. The authors read this as continuity and an eastward move of people, not collapse.

Technical detail

Macrobotanical analysis with direct dating of grains and seeds; settlement 4,300-3,400 yr BP; the Bara culture emerged around 2300 BCE, alongside the late Urban phase. Winter and summer crops, legumes in both seasons (crop rotation), a directly dated rice grain. One site; “migration” is inferred from material similarity (abstract only).

What we take from it

Background

Late inscriptions are rare. This supports asking whether writing faded with the cities or moved east with the people. It also helps date late-phase objects.
